claim: The surgical history reports, in the case of Private S. T. Newell, wounded at Gettysburg on July 2, 1863 and entered at the Satterlee Hospital, Philadelphia, on July 11th, that a severe flesh wound of the thigh made by a piece of shell was first dressed simply, assumed a gangrenous appearance on the 19th, and was treated with a mixture of equal parts of creasote, alcohol and water.

source.edition: Part III, Volume II, Surgical History, first issue, Washington: Government Printing Office, 1883 (chapters X to XV: lower extremities, miscellaneous injuries, complications, anaesthetics, the medical staff and materia chirurgica, transportation of the wounded)

quote: Private S. T. Newell, Co. B ... was wounded at Gettysburg, July 2, 1863, and entered the Satterlee Hospital, Philadelphia, July 11th ... The missile, a piece of shell, struck the inner side of the left thigh, middle third, producing a severe flesh wound. Simple dressings were applied. On the 19th the wound assumed a gangrenous appearance; a mixture of equal parts of creasote, alcohol, and water was applied.

data.name_period: a mixture of equal parts of creasote, alcohol and water applied to a gangrenous wound

scene.may_show: A thigh wound dressed with a mixture of equal parts of creasote, alcohol and water, in a general hospital.
scene.reduced_form: a dressed thigh under a sheet

notes: Satterlee Hospital, Philadelphia (a general hospital): the patient entered it on July 11th; the month of the 19th is read from that context, no month is printed with the 19th
